title: Work with a range of patterns and functions and solve problems

lessons.title: Seeing number patterns at work
lessons.html:
What is a pattern?

A pattern is something that repeats or grows in a regular way. When you can see the pattern, you can predict what comes next. Patterns help us plan work.

Repeating patterns

Think of shift rosters. If a team works day shift, day shift, night shift, night shift, off, off, and then repeats, you can work out which shift you will work in three weeks. This is a repeating pattern of 6 days.

Growing patterns

Some patterns grow by the same amount each time. At a poultry plant, a crate holds 12 birds. Look at the pattern:

Crates12345
Birds1224364860

Each time we add one crate, we add 12 birds. The rule is: birds = 12 × crates. With this rule you can work out 20 crates without counting: 12 × 20 = 240 birds.

Finding the rule

  1. Look at how much the numbers change each step.
  2. If they change by the same amount, that amount is the multiplier.
  3. Check if something is added at the start. For example, a delivery costs R200 call-out plus R15 per bag. 1 bag = R215, 2 bags = R230, 3 bags = R245. The rule is: cost = 200 + 15 × bags.
  4. Test your rule on a number you already know.

Patterns are everywhere: the number of carcasses per hour, kilograms of grain per load, or bags stacked on a pallet. Once you know the rule, you can solve problems quickly and check if something is wrong.

lessons.title: Rules, tables and graphs
lessons.html:
Showing a relationship in different ways

A rule that links two things is called a function. We can show the same function in words, as a formula, as a table or as a graph.

Example: water use for cleaning

A hose uses 20 litres of water per minute.

  • In words: the water used is 20 litres for every minute the hose runs.
  • Formula: litres = 20 × minutes
  • Table:
Minutes051015
Litres0100200300

Drawing a graph

  1. Draw a line across the bottom (horizontal axis) for minutes.
  2. Draw a line up the side (vertical axis) for litres.
  3. Mark each pair from the table as a dot, such as 5 minutes and 100 litres.
  4. Join the dots. Here the dots make a straight line.

A straight line means the amount grows by the same amount each time. A steeper line means it grows faster. If a second hose used 30 litres per minute, its line would be steeper.

Reading a graph

To read a graph, find the value on the bottom axis, go straight up to the line, then go across to the side axis and read the answer. Graphs on the notice board might show daily throughput, rejected product, or water use for the week. Look for days that are much higher or lower than normal. They may show a problem, such as a leaking pipe.

Saving water matters on South African farms and plants because water is scarce. Knowing your water use helps you save it.

lessons.title: Solving everyday problems
lessons.html:
Using patterns to solve problems

Maths at work is about solving real problems. Follow these steps:

  1. Read the problem and find what you must work out.
  2. Write down the facts you know.
  3. Find the rule or pattern.
  4. Work it out.
  5. Check that the answer makes sense.

Problem 1: Grain bags

A pallet holds 40 bags of maize meal. How many pallets do you need for 520 bags?

Rule: pallets = bags ÷ 40. 520 ÷ 40 = 13 pallets. Check: 13 × 40 = 520. Correct.

Problem 2: Overtime pay

A worker earns R30 per hour, and overtime is paid at one and a half times the normal rate. How much is 4 hours of overtime?

Overtime rate = R30 × 1.5 = R45 per hour. 4 hours × R45 = R180.

Problem 3: Line speed

A slaughter line processes 60 sheep per hour. How long will it take for 450 sheep?

Time = 450 ÷ 60 = 7.5 hours, which is 7 hours and 30 minutes.

Check if the answer makes sense

Always ask: is this answer sensible? If you work out that one worker packs 5 000 boxes in one hour, you have probably made a mistake. Estimate first. 450 sheep at about 60 per hour is a bit less than 8 hours, so 7.5 hours sounds right.

Key points

  • A pattern repeats or grows in a regular way.
  • Find the rule by looking at how much the numbers change each step.
  • A function can be shown in words, as a formula, a table or a graph.
  • A straight line graph means the same increase each step.
  • Always estimate and check that your answer makes sense.
